slides: Let's continue, and work with letters.

slides.say: Sometimes the average is equal to one of the letters. We do the same thing, we write the sum.
The average of x, y and z is x. So the sum is three times x. x plus y plus z is equal to three x.
at: The average of x, y and z is x
x plus y plus z is equal

slides.say: We take x away from both sides. So y plus z is equal to two x.
at: So y plus z is equal

slides.say: Two numbers with a sum of two x have an average of x. So y and z also have an average of x.
One more. The average of m and n is equal to their difference, m minus n. Then the sum is two times the difference.
at: The average of m and n
Then the sum is two times

slides.say: Careful, two times the whole difference. That's two m minus two n.
at: That's two m minus two n

slides.say: We add two n to both sides, and take m away from both sides. So three n is equal to m.
Let's check with numbers. n is two, so m is six. Their sum is eight, and the average is four. The difference is six minus two, also four.
at: The difference is six minus two

slides.say: The balance also works with more than and less than. The average of a, b and c is more than six. The average of a, b, c and d is less than six. What must be true?
at: The average of a, b and c is more
The average of a, b, c and d

slides: Think of six as a line. a, b and c are above the line on average. So together they have something extra above six.
But all four together are below the line. So someone pulls them down, by more than that extra. Only d is left. So d must be less than six.

slides.say: Let's check with sums. a plus b plus c is more than three times six, eighteen.
And all four add up to less than four times six, twenty-four.
So d is less than twenty-four minus eighteen, six.

What about a alone? It can be below six. For example, a is two, b is nine, and c is ten. Their sum is twenty-one, and twenty-one divided by three is seven, above six. Choose d as one. The four add up to twenty-two, divided by four, five point five. That's below six, so both givens hold.
at: a is two, b is nine
divided by four, five point five

slides.say: So a doesn't have to be above six. Only d is sure. When they ask what must be true, test the other letters with numbers.
at: When they ask what must be true

slides.say: Let's sum up. The sum is equal to how many numbers there are, times the average.
at: The sum is equal to how many

slides.say: When a number joins or leaves, and they ask how many, compare it to the average of the group it is in.
When they ask for the newcomer or the new average, share its distance from the old average among the new group.
at: When they ask for the newcomer

slides.say: For the biggest possible value, make the others as small as they can be.
And with letters, plug in equal values, or write the sum.

slides: Take a moment to memorize this. Now let's use it in the questions. I'll see you in the next video.
